newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Bunds to waltz as high yielders rumba.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Bunds to waltz as high yielders rumba.

text.p: Robust economic data from Germany should not prove too troublesome for Bunds on second reading, but investors will find better value in more lively markets, analysts said on Thursday.

High yielders and Britain offer better potential for gains in the medium term than sleepy Bunds, they said. Investors may be wise to play derivatives market however, with U.S. interest rate movements likely to cause ructions.
"We still favour the high yielders in the next few months," said Stephen King, chief European economist at HSBC James Capel.

"Obviously there will be some nervousness in the short term as to what the reaction might be to any U.S. rate increase next week," said King, based in London. "Once that's out of the way we're still very much in an environment of low interest rates."
German bond markets skidded early on Thursday as fresh data showed money supply grew an annualised 8.7 percent in August, above forecasts for 8.0 percent and against July's 8.6 percent.

But the market erased some of its losses after a report from the Ifo economics institute. Ifo's west German business climate index registered 94.4 in August, compared with forecasts of 94.5 and only slightly above the 94.0 in July.

Analysts said the net effect would not be dramatic for Bunds, and unlikely to drive the 10-year yield far from a 6.14 percent trough it reached on Tuesday. The yield had not been that low since the middle of February.
While the M3 data were worrying they came against a backdrop of weaker statistics painting a still poorly economy, said King.
Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London, said a close reading showed M3 was not a great inflation threat.
"It all points to this EMU (European Economic and Monetary Union) effect," said Reed. "German savers are reluctant to hold instruments that expire post-EMU."
She added deposit growth has been picking up just as much as capital formation has been slowing down.
The Bundesbank said banks received 7.2 billion marks in long term funds from domestic sources this month compared with 17.6 billion marks a year ago.
While Bunds should continue to thrive in such an environment analysts said larger gains could be squeezed out of the high yielding markets.
"The outlook for German monetary policy is pretty secure and consequently that should underpin some of the high yielders," said King, favouring Italy.

BZW's Reed also recommended investors avoid Germany in favour of high yielders, despite their outperformance in recent months. "If you're in the high yielders you probably want to switch your Spanish and Swedish exposure to Italy were there's more value," she added.

The BTP/Bund spread has dipped below 300 basis points this week, a level it had been above since the end of July. But Reed said that represented good value with inflation expected to dip below three percent next year and the potential for interest rate cuts too high to resist.
BZW is also favouring gilts after shunning the British market for two years, said Mark Capleton, international bond strategist at BZW.

He said the market has a long way to catch up after lagging high yielders this year. Meanwhile a victory by the opposition Labour party in the next election -- historically seen as more negative for markets than the Conservatives -- was fairly well priced into yields, he added.
BZW has a 12-month target of 125 basis points on the gilt/Bund 10-year yield spread but Capleton said most of the gains will come after the election. The gap is currently at 177.
Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Capital Markets, said high yielders had their charms but he would not go wholesale into those markets.
"Any further exposure you want to do in peripheral markets is probably best played by buying call options rather than committing fresh cash," he said.

"For the sake of the last 20 basis points I think the risk reward is increasingly suggesting once the external problem of the stronger dollar is removed, there will be a very different picture emerging in 1997," he said.
